extracted.intended_audience: users of the PARI/GP computer-algebra system (mathematicians, computational number theorists, and GP programmers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and rules for entering expressions, choosing and using GP data types, operators, variables, and for writing multi-line GP code. Covers input syntax, type-specific behaviors, efficiency cautions, operator precedence, and variable/namespace rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Line continuation rules
rubrics_metrics.description: How to continue expressions on the next line: use a trailing backslash \\ immediately followed by a newline; an equal sign at line end is disregarded (useful when defining a user function); or enclose multi-line commands in braces { }.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Backslash must be immediately followed by a newline (apart from ignored whitespace). Examples: ? 3 + \\ \n4 instead of 3 + 4. If an = ends a line it is ignored: ? a = \n123 gives %1 = 123. Prefer the brace form for multi-line programs but observe brace restrictions (see next).

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiline-brace rules and pitfalls
rubrics_metrics.description: An opening brace { signals a multi-line command; newlines are ignored until the matching } and all input lines inside are concatenated (newlines suppressed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two restrictions: braces do not nest; and inside { } all lines are concatenated, so newlines should occur only after a semicolon, a comma, or an operator. Do not split an identifier across lines. Anti-pattern: writing { a = b \n b = c } becomes a=bb=c and silently produces incorrect results. Correct: { a = b; b = c; }.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convenience types vs. efficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Types t_INTMOD, t_FRAC, t_PADIC, t_QUAD, t_POLMOD, t_RFRAC are provided for convenience but are not always fastest because they perform reductions after each basic operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For recursive objects or heavy computations prefer libpari (C) or use integer-only strategies (cancel denominators) and homomorphic/modular methods. Example: working modularly with Mod(...) can be dramatically faster than using large rationals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integer input syntax
rubrics_metrics.description: Integers: optional leading + or -, decimal digits, no decimal point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may input hex with 0x prefix (hex digits a..f upper/lowercase allowed) and binary with 0b prefix. Examples: ? 1234567, ? -3, ? 0xF, ? 0b010101.

rubrics_metrics.name: Real number input and precision behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Real numbers (t_REAL) require a decimal point (or scientific notation) and acquire an internal precision determined by the input and default realprecision; trailing zeros matter for declared input precision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scientific notation with E/e allowed (e.g. 6.02E23 or 1e-5). 0.En returns a zero real with exponent n; 0. returns a zero of default precision (machine epsilon). Use realprecision (\p) or realbitprecision (\ps) to inspect/change global precision interactively; in programs prefer localbitprec to adapt precision locally. If integer part is unknown due to exponent vs precision, GP prints in e format.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creation and semantics of intmods (t_INTMOD)
rubrics_metrics.description: Create residue class Mod(a,b) (image of integer a in Z/bZ); do not use a % b for this.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Internally operations use representatives in [0,b-1]. This type is convenient but slower because each elementary operation reduces modulo b. Member function x.mod returns the modulus b.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rational numbers (t_FRAC) input and behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Fractions are automatically reduced to lowest terms; input n/m as written. No floating point division occurs for rationals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rational arithmetic is often slower because each elementary operation computes a gcd. Prefer cancelling denominators and working with integers, or use modular/homomorphic approaches. Examples illustrate that computing sums modulo p with Mod(1/i,p) is far faster than doing the rational sum then reducing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite field elements (t_FFELT) construction and members
rubrics_metrics.description: Build finite fields with ffinit and generators with ffgen(T,'y); the second parameter affects display only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the resulting generator to build elements. Member functions: g.pol (polynomial expressing g in field generator), g.p (characteristic), g.f (degree of extension), g.mod (minimal polynomial). Example: T = ffinit(2,8); y = ffgen(T,'y).

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex numbers notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use I (uppercase) for the imaginary unit: enter x + I*y to represent x + i*y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Real and imaginary parts can be t_INT, t_REAL, t_INTMOD, t_FRAC, or t_PADIC. Note: I is the constant satisfying I^2 = -1.

rubrics_metrics.name: p-adic input and precautions (t_PADIC)
rubrics_metrics.description: Type O(p^k) to obtain a p-adic 0 of accuracy k; input a p-adic number as a suitable integer/rational approximation plus O(p^k).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GP does not check that p is prime; using composite p leads to undefined/broken behavior (examples provided). O(25) is not the same as O(5^2) — use explicit p^k. Member functions: a.mod returns pk, a.p returns p. t_PADICs are convenient but slow because pk updates and reductions occur on each operation; for speed consider t_INTMODs where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quadratic number type (t_QUAD) usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Use w = quadgen(d,'w) to assign the canonical generator w of the quadratic order of discriminant d; input elements as x + y*w.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware that t_QUADs with different discriminants may be printed similarly but are not equal; GP will refuse incompatible operations. The member function z.disc retrieves discriminant d; real(z) and imag(z) give coefficients x and y. You may work in the fraction field Q(sqrt(d)) using t_FRAC for coefficients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polynomial-mod (t_POLMOD) creation and variable/priority constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Create polynomial residue classes with Mod(x,y) (not x%y). Polmods perform reductions modulo y and are represented as polynomials in an internal variable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Polmods are convenient but slower (reductions on each op). Variables occurring in a polmod are not free; internal computations use the representative of lowest degree, in a specific internal variable. To avoid inconsistencies, polmods mixed in operations must use the same variable internally; otherwise results may be surprising. Mixing t_POL and t_POLMOD is allowed if the main variables match.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polynomial (t_POL) input and best practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Type polynomials naturally; remember to put * between a coefficient and a formal variable. Use 'x to denote a free variable independent of any binding in the session.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid assigning values to polynomial variable names (x = 1) to prevent accidental evaluation to integers. Use 'x or Pol/Polrev constructors for safer and more efficient construction. Polrev/Pol constructors are linear-time and much faster than explicit summations (quadratic). Polynomials are printed univariately with monomials sorted by decreasing degree.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power series (t_SER) input and caveats
rubrics_metrics.description: Use O(X^k) to create an X-adic 0 of accuracy k and input a series as a polynomial/rational plus O(X^k).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caveat: power series with inexact coefficients may behave unintuitively: an inexact zero can be considered significant, leading to discarding useful higher-order terms. If a series with zero leading coefficient must be inverted, GP attempts normalization and issues a warning. Insufficient series precision can cause division-by-zero and other errors; understanding global precision is important to avoid these problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rational functions (t_RFRAC) behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Rational functions are always reduced to lowest terms on input and follow the same considerations as fractions (t_FRAC).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use same performance considerations as for t_FRAC: gcds on each operation can be costly; consider alternatives for heavy computation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Binary quadratic forms (t_QFR/t_QFI) construction and accessors
rubrics_metrics.description: Create binary quadratic forms via Qfb(a,b,c); discriminant via poldisc and components via Vec or component() functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imaginary forms (negative discriminant) are implemented as t_QFI with only positive-definite implemented. For positive discriminant (t_QFR) an optional fourth component relates to regulator/distance (Shanks-Lenstra). Use qfbprimeform to create a prime form of given discriminant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vectors (t_VEC) and column vectors (t_COL) syntax and indexing
rubrics_metrics.description: Row vectors: [a,b,c]; column vectors: type horizontally then transpose with ~. Indexing: v[m], slices v[i..j], removal v[^i]; negative indices count from the end (-1 is last).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can assign to v[m] but not to slices v[i..j] or v[^i]. Use vector(...) and vectorv(...) constructors for automatic sequences; Vec/Col convert objects. Alternative set-notation comprehensions [g(x) | x <- v, f(x)] and shortcuts exist for apply/select patterns and are useful constructors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Matrix (t_MAT) syntax, indexing and internal representation caveats
rubrics_metrics.description: Matrices: enter components row-by-row with commas and semicolons inside [ ]. Indexing: M[i,j] entry, M[i,] row, M[,j] column; M[i] is invalid. Range and caret notations for submatrices exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submatrix extraction forms include M[i..j,k..l], M[i..j,], M[,i..j], M[i..j,^k] etc. M[i..j,k] returns a t_COL, M[k,i..j] returns a t_VEC. Internal representation is a vector of columns; matrices with 0 columns are represented by the same object, so matrices with zero columns and nonzero rows cannot be distinguished — be mindful of the empty matrix [;] behavior. A row vector of column vectors is not a matrix; use Vec/Mat to convert representations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lists (t_LIST) creation and mutation
rubrics_metrics.description: Lists can be created as List([1,2,3]) or by making an empty list and appending elements with listput.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Access elements similarly to vectors. Example: a = List(); listput(a,1); listput(a,2); prints as List([1,2]).

rubrics_metrics.name: Strings (t_STR) representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Strings are enclosed in double quotes "..."; Str() converts objects to strings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard string input/output; use Str(object) when converting non-string objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functions (t_CLOSURE) creation forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Functions (closures) can be created via f = (x,y) -> expr or by defining f(x,y) = expr.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functions are first-class objects and can be assigned to variables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Error contexts (t_ERROR) and exception handling
rubrics_metrics.description: t_ERROR objects are created when an error occurs; GP prints an error and aborts the computation entering a break loop unless exceptions are trapped.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use iferr(expression, E, handler) to catch exceptions: you can ignore, print, extract information (component(E,i)), or rethrow with error(E). Example: i = Mod(6,12); iferr(1/i, E, print(E)); 1 + 1 continues after handling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinity objects (t_INFINITY)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are only two infinity objects +oo and -oo; they can be compared to finite reals but not involved in arithmetic operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparisons with t_INFINITY are allowed; expressions like 1+oo are errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: GP operator priorities and associativity
rubrics_metrics.description: Operators have fixed and unchangeable priorities; unless noted, operators at the same priority are left-associative, assignments are right-associative. Parentheses override precedence. Unary operators may be prefix or postfix with different semantics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When in doubt, use parentheses for clarity. Examples of consequences: a + b + c parsed as (a + b) + c (left-assoc); a = b = c parsed as a = (b = c) (right-assoc). Some operator symbols mean different things in prefix vs postfix positions (e.g. ! prefix is logical not, ! postfix is factorial).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific operator semantics and noteworthy differences from C
rubrics_metrics.description: GP supports many operators: ++/-- (postfix, behave like C prefix ++ by returning new value), selection operator [ ], derivative ' (postfix), transpose ~, factorial ! (postfix), logical not ! (prefix), cardinality #, power ^ (right-associative), exact division /, Euclidean quotient/remainder \, %, rounded quotient \/, binary shifts << >> etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of differences vs C: postfix ++ in GP returns the new value (like C's prefix ++). << and >> have different priorities than in C. For selection and assignment, parentheses can change lvalue status: x[1][1] = 0 is valid but (x[1])[1] = 0 is invalid because parentheses force evaluation to a non-modifiable value. Use op= operators (e.g., +=, *=) for legibility; note op= results are not lvalues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment semantics and deep copy behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: The = operator is assignment (not equality test). The result of x = y is the value y, which is assigned to x. Assignment is deep copy for all variables; left-hand side must be an lvalue else parse error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equality test operator is ==. Assignment operators op= (e.g., +=, *=) assign x op y to x and return the new value but are not lvalues. Example: 1 + x = 1 is parsed as 1 + (x = 1) and is valid; x + 1 = 1 is a syntax error because left side is not an lvalue. Assigning to local variables releases space when out of scope or when the value changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advice on using op= and ++/-- for legibility and speed
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer op= and ++/-- operators to make complex assignments more legible; ++/-- may be slightly more efficient in common loops.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: v[i+j-1]++ is clearer than v[i+j-1] = v[i+j-1] + 1. Benchmarks show small differences; op= may sometimes be less efficient (measured examples given). Use them for readability and measure if performance-critical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variable naming rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Valid variable names start with a letter followed by letters or digits; built-in function names and reserved constants (Pi, Euler, Catalan, I, oo) are reserved and cannot be used. GP names are case sensitive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can use up to 16383 variable names (65535 on 64-bit). If you need thousands of variables, prefer storing them in vectors (e.g., X[1], X[2], ...).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quote operator and free variables ('t)
rubrics_metrics.description: The quote operator 't registers a new free variable (symbol) t with the interpreter and evaluates to a monomial of degree 1 in that variable. Using an uninitialized name implicitly yields 'name (backward compatibility).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To avoid accidental binding/mis-evaluation, explicitly use 't or initialize t = 't before using t. Substitution pitfalls: if you construct p = t^2 + 1 with 't and later bind t = 2, subst(p, t, 3) fails unless you used subst(p, 't, 3). Use 't to make expressions robust to later assignments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variable priorities and multivariate object ordering
rubrics_metrics.description: Variables are implicitly ordered by the interpreter: when a new identifier is registered, it gets a lower priority than variables already in use. Multivariate polynomials are stored as univariate polynomials whose coefficients are polynomials in lower-priority variables; the highest-priority variable is the main variable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The internal variable ordering affects operations like Euclidean division and Mod(...) behavior. Use variable() to inspect ordering. To get a desired ordering, declare variables in the preferred order at session start (e.g., 'x; 'y; 'z;) or use varhigher/varlower to create variables with specific priorities. Important note: GP assumes Euclidean division happens in the fraction field of the coefficient ring — this can produce surprising results if coefficients are not in an integral domain; be mindful when mixing rings/fields (examples shown).
